solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

indicatorNotes.beheaded: loses its head, the first letter
indicatorNotes.condemned: the letters are sentenced to be broken up

annotation.surface: A gangster called Benny Malone, beheaded like a condemned queen of old.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Condemned Queen' reads as one phrase describing the answer, but 'condemned' is the anagram instruction and 'Queen' alone is the definition. Anne Boleyn, Henry VIII's second wife, was beheaded in 1536.
annotation.definitionFit: Anne Boleyn was Queen of England as Henry VIII's second wife.

entries.clue: Boats in flotilla discover Greek ships last of all (4)

indicatorNotes.last of all: take the last letter of every word

blocks.note: the last letters of flotillA discoveR GreeK shipS

annotation.surface: Someone finds Greek ships at the back of a flotilla.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boats in flotilla' looks like a single phrase, but 'in' is only the join: 'Boats' is the definition and the four words after it supply one letter each.
annotation.definitionFit: An ark is a boat, most famously Noah's.

entries.clue: Bird run over crossing motorway in German metropolis (9)

indicatorNotes.over: turned over, so the letters run backwards
indicatorNotes.crossing: the reversed letters span the M, holding it inside

blocks.note: the grebe is a diving water bird

annotation.surface: A bird runs out across a motorway somewhere in a big German city.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Run over' tempts you towards roadkill, which suits the motorway; in fact 'over' turns the bird and the run round together as one string.
annotation.definitionFit: Nuremberg is a large city in Bavaria, Germany.

indicatorNotes.start to: take the first letter of the next word

annotation.surface: Backers start to spend money.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Supporters' reads as fans or financial backers, which suits the money; it is underwear. Brass is British slang for money, as in 'where there's muck there's brass'.
annotation.definitionFit: Brass is informal British slang for money.

entries.clue: Somewhere up north, boy holds map (7)

indicatorNotes.holds: the first word keeps the second inside it

blocks.note: a plan can be a map, as of a building

annotation.surface: A boy clutches a map somewhere in the far north.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Somewhere up north' is vague on purpose: a definition by example, and the answer lies well beyond the north of England the phrase suggests.
annotation.definitionFit: Lapland is the region of northern Scandinavia and Finland inside the Arctic Circle.

blocks.note: something that shows when a time has arrived, like a clock
rum reads as odd, as in 'rum times'; it is the drink, and the times are drinking times

annotation.surface: Something that signals times that are rum, meaning odd or strange.
annotation.walkthrough: By sailors' tradition, once the sun is over the yardarm, the end of a ship's spar, it is time for the first drink of the day.
annotation.definitionFit: The sun passing the yardarm marks the hour when drinking can start, so it indicates rum time.

indicatorNotes.rejected: sent back, so its letters run the other way

blocks.note: SP is the starting price, the odds on a horse
an MA is a Master of Arts

annotation.surface: A postgraduate student turns down some chances and some processed food.
annotation.walkthrough: SP, starting price, is the betting odds on a horse at the off, so 'chances'.
annotation.definitionFit: A brand name used as a plain noun: the tinned pork luncheon meat is the best-known processed food.

entries.clue: Too good a number for music-maker (5)

blocks.note: pi, short for pious, is sanctimonious

annotation.surface: A number that is too good to be played by a musician.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Number' looks like a piece of music, which suits the music-maker; it only gives NO. PI is informal British for smugly pious, which is being too good.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by function: the instrument is described by what it does.

entries.clue: State of Oregon meant, unusually, to deport American (10)

indicatorNotes.unusually: the letters are set in an unusual order
indicatorNotes.to deport: the A is sent out of the letters

blocks.note: A is short for American; it is removed

annotation.surface: A US state official means, oddly, to throw out an American.
annotation.walkthrough: 'State of Oregon' reads as one phrase, suggesting a US state; the definition is 'State' alone and the fodder starts at Oregon.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Balkan country is one sovereign state among many.

indicatorNotes.Sounding: the answer sounds like the word that follows

blocks.note: more relaxed = calmer, said with a southern British accent that drops the R

annotation.surface: Someone who sounds calmer puts it down to fate.
annotation.walkthrough: The homophone relies on a non-rhotic British accent, where the L of 'calmer' is silent and neither word sounds an R.
annotation.definitionFit: Karma is the idea that one's actions decide one's fate, so destiny.

entries.clue: Beer batch returned in fine containers? (9)

indicatorNotes.returned: sent back, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: a crop is a batch, as of students

annotation.surface: A batch of beer is sent back because it arrived in fancy containers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like the join to the definition but is part of the wordplay, added after the reversal. The question mark flags a looser definition: porcelain is the material of fine china pots.
annotation.definitionFit: Fine china cups and bowls are porcelain, so porcelain can stand for fine containers.

indicatorNotes.burst: the letters are burst apart and rearranged

annotation.surface: A child reports popping the bouncy castle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bouncy castle' is a fixed phrase, so it is hard to split 'Bouncy' off as the definition. 'Burst' suits the inflatable perfectly.
annotation.definitionFit: Something elastic springs back, which is bouncy.

entries.clue: War paint mum used to cover a mark (7)

indicatorNotes.used to cover: the letters of mum go round the others

annotation.surface: Mother applies war paint to hide a scar.
annotation.walkthrough: 'War paint' is jokey slang for make-up, not battle colours.
annotation.definitionFit: Slang meets example: war paint is jokey slang for make-up, and this eye cosmetic is one kind.

indicatorNotes.we hear: what is heard, not what is spelt

annotation.surface: A declaration of love at a doorway.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Love' could be a noun or a verb; the homophone fixes it as a verb. In a British accent the two are said alike.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as a verb: to worship someone is a strong form of loving them.

blocks.note: reads as a man's name; it is a punctuation mark
reads as a London station district; it means taken out of the words King's Cross as printed

annotation.surface: Someone called Mark comes from King's Cross, the London station district.
annotation.walkthrough: King's Cross is a London railway station, so 'Mark' reads as a man's name. Read literally, the question is which mark appears in the words 'King's Cross'.
annotation.definitionFit: The apostrophe is the punctuation mark that sits in 'King's'.

entries.clue: Happy first of prisoners let out (7)

indicatorNotes.first of: the first of a word is its opening letter

annotation.surface: The first prisoners to be released are happy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Let out' reads as freed from jail; it means rented, as in a flat let out to tenants.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe contentment.

blocks.note: a bank is an example of a lender

annotation.surface: London's South Bank is a narrow strip along the Thames.
annotation.walkthrough: 'South Bank' reads as the London riverside arts district, so it is hard to split into a direction and a bank.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a slender margin or waist is a narrow one.

entries.clue: Artist engaged by diplomat is second-rate (7)

indicatorNotes.engaged by: the answer is held within the following words

annotation.surface: A painter taken on by a diplomat turns out to be second-rate.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Engaged' reads as hired, which suits a diplomat commissioning a painting; it means held inside.
annotation.definitionFit: Henri Matisse was a French painter.

entries.clue: Reptile devouring collection of fowl that’s cold (9)

annotation.definitionNote: a clause standing for 'something that's cold'

indicatorNotes.collection of: the letters of fowl are gathered in a new order
indicatorNotes.devouring: the reptile swallows the other letters

annotation.surface: A snake eats a clutch of chickens, which leaves it cold.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Collection of fowl' reads as a flock, but 'collection' is the anagram instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A snowflake is a crystal of ice, something that is cold.

entries.clue: Part of group infiltrated by FBI agents (7)

indicatorNotes.infiltrated by: the second part gets inside the first

annotation.surface: A faction of a group has been penetrated by the FBI.
annotation.walkthrough: G-men, short for Government men, is old American slang for FBI agents.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a segment of an orange is one part of it.

indicatorNotes.Inside: the rearranged letters go inside the other word
indicatorNotes.unusual: the letters of one are put in an unusual order

blocks.note: to dog someone is to tail them

annotation.surface: Some unusual growth has been found inside a dog.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dog' reads as an animal with a growth inside it; it is a verb meaning to follow. 'Growth' suggests a tumour, but the answer is simply something that grows.
annotation.definitionFit: A toenail keeps growing, so it counts as a growth.

indicatorNotes.picked up: picked up as a signal or a remark is picked up, by ear

blocks.note: a mug is a sucker, someone easily fooled

annotation.surface: Someone offers help while picking up a coffee mug.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mug' reads as a cup, which suits 'picked up'; it is British slang for a gullible person.
annotation.definitionFit: Succour is help given in time of need.

blocks.note: p, piano, is quiet in music

annotation.surface: A shady gang is keeping us quiet.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'us' the victims of a gang; the word is simply lifted into the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: British informal: something dodgy is of doubtful honesty, and that is suspect as an adjective.

indicatorNotes.in: the letter goes inside the word

blocks.note: p is the physics symbol for power

annotation.surface: A naval fleet shows its might in an assault.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fleet' reads as a navy, which suits the attack; it is the adjective meaning fast.
annotation.definitionFit: Fleet as an adjective means swift, so rapid.

indicatorNotes.initially: at the start, so the opening letter of the word

annotation.surface: The amount of poetry being written has gone up.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'Writing poetry' one phrase, so prose, its opposite, hides behind it.
annotation.definitionFit: Prose is ordinary written language, writing that is not verse.

indicatorNotes.inside: the answer sits inside the words before it

annotation.surface: Someone begs an official to calm down, since the official is already in.
annotation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark and apostrophe break the surface into a plea, which hides the letters running across 'please! Official'.
annotation.definitionFit: A phrasal verb as synonym: to stop pushing so hard, to slacken.

blocks.note: a live wire is electrically charged

annotation.surface: Nobody pays anything for the fruit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Charged' reads as billed, which pairs with 'nothing' for free fruit; it means electrically live.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example, and a botanical one: the stone-bearing olive is a fruit, though eaten like a vegetable.

annotation.surface: Someone takes advantage of a lucky twist of fate.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Exploit' reads as a verb, to take advantage; it is the noun, a bold deed.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the noun sense: a daring deed or achievement.

indicatorNotes.rewrite: the letters are written again in another order

annotation.surface: A teacher makes the children redo an excellent school report.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Make children' reads as forcing pupils to do something; it is the definition, meaning to have children.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain paraphrase: producing offspring is literally making children.

entries.clue: Cross buccaneer having lost parrot at first (5)

indicatorNotes.having lost: a buccaneer who has lost something no longer has it, so the letter goes
indicatorNotes.at first: what comes first in a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: the first letter of Parrot, removed

annotation.surface: An angry pirate has lost his parrot.
annotation.walkthrough: A parrot suits a pirate so well that it hides being only a letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: cross as an adjective means angry.

entries.clue: Idyllic place: country, not Devon and Cornwall? (4)

indicatorNotes.not: the country without these letters, as in 'country, not SW'

blocks.note: Devon and Cornwall are counties in England's South West, SW

annotation.surface: A perfect country retreat, as long as it is not in Devon or Cornwall.
annotation.walkthrough: Devon and Cornwall make up the far South West of England; the question mark marks them as an example of that region.
annotation.definitionFit: Eden, the garden of Genesis, stands for any idyllic place.

entries.clue: Cheers giant cycling around ancient city (3,3,4)

indicatorNotes.cycling: the first letter moves to the end
indicatorNotes.around: the result goes round the city

blocks.note: TALL, with its T cycled to the end
Thebes was a city of ancient Greece and of ancient Egypt

annotation.surface: A giant rides a bicycle round an ancient city.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Giant' is an adjective here, meaning very big, not a creature from a story.
annotation.definitionFit: 'All the best!' is a farewell or toast, like 'Cheers!'
